summary: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a free, bilingual (English/Portuguese) browser game that teaches young students how space missions are engineered by letting them make the decisions themselves. Students command a small outpost at the lunar south pole: they pack a lander within a fixed launch-mass budget, then keep a crew of four alive through terrain-shadow periods, solar storms, leaks and equipment failures. Every choice is a trade-off: more batteries mean fewer supplies, more shielding means less room for a greenhouse. The simulation is driven by documented values from NASA sources, such as oxygen use per astronaut (NASA BVAD), ISS water recovery rates and NASA crew radiation limits, and every number is labelled as a law of nature, a measurement, an engineering reference or a game estimate. When the mission ends, the game explains why it succeeded or failed and lets students replay the same start to compare decisions. Trade-offs that usually appear in charts and reports become an experience students play through.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a mission-engineering simulator for young students. The player chooses a rank (Cadet to Commander) and a mission at the lunar south pole (First Light at Shackleton, 12 days, or Artemis Base Camp, 28 days), then:

1. Packs the lander within a mass budget: solar arrays, batteries, water recycler, oxygen generator (electrolysis), greenhouse, radiation shelter, and supplies of water, oxygen, food and spare kits. Before launch, a projection shows the margins of the chosen loadout.

2. Runs the outpost day by day. The engine computes solar power (following the mission's light and shadow calendar), battery storage, crew consumption, recycling, production and radiation dose. When power runs short, systems are shut down by priority.

3. Faces events (NOAA S3/S4 solar storms, cabin air leak, water leak, dust on solar arrays, equipment and crop failures) and chooses between options with explicit costs and benefits, such as moving the crew into the regolith-shielded shelter during a storm.

4. Gets a mission report: why the mission succeeded or failed, charts of supplies and radiation dose, each decision told as a short story, a science lesson, and a "replay with the same start" mode that compares two attempts side by side.

There is a management view and an immersive first-person view inside the habitat, with lunar-gravity movement (1.62 m/s²), staged emergencies and an optional countdown for urgent decisions.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Space-mission engineering is a chain of trade-offs that students usually only see as results in charts. Here they make the trade-offs and feel the consequences, which builds systems thinking, data literacy and interest in STEM careers. The game is free, runs in any browser with no install or account, and is available in English and Portuguese, so it can reach Portuguese-speaking classrooms such as ours in Angola. Accessibility was a design goal: a contextual glossary (mSv, kWh, regolith, electrolysis), a skippable tutorial, a "no time pressure" mode, and a visual equivalent for every sound.

SCIENTIFIC GROUNDING

Every parameter is documented in science.json with its source and classified as a law of nature, a measurement in space, an engineering reference or a game estimate. Examples: 0.84 kg of O2 per astronaut per day (NASA BVAD), 93% water recovery (ISS ECLSS), 1.125 kg of water per kg of O2 (electrolysis stoichiometry), 1.37 mSv/day of cosmic-ray dose on the lunar surface (Chang'e-4), and a 250 mSv mission limit inspired by NASA-STD-3001. The game states its simplifications openly (for example, storm doses are scenario estimates). An offline Python script checks that the game data matches the documented parameters.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

TypeScript, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, Three.js (3D outpost and habitat), Web Audio API (all sounds generated procedurally, no audio files), Vite, Vitest (unit, i18n and Monte Carlo balance tests) and Python 3 (science validation). The deterministic, seeded simulation engine is separate from the UI. All textures, icons and artwork are generated in code, with no third-party image assets. Open source under the MIT licence.

CREATIVITY

Instead of showing data, the project turns it into gameplay: the player experiences the oxygen budget, the shadow periods and the solar storm dose. The deterministic replay lets students run their own controlled experiment ("what if I had brought one more battery?"). Sound follows the ISS Caution & Warning philosophy, and the 3D scene respects lunar physics: a black sky, no dust clouds and long polar shadows.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty (labelling estimates as estimates), age-appropriate language, accessibility, bilingual support, running offline in a browser with no backend or personal data, replayability, and mission balance (tested with Monte Carlo simulations so missions are challenging but winnable).
